demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Going to or near the place where the event happened
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed
I have failed in my most important role in life

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: For a trauma defined as accidentally causing serious injury to another, 'Avoid Perpetrator Cues' is hard to reconcile because it implies the patient was harmed by a perpetrator rather than being the agent who injured someone else. That is a direct mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Humiliation' is not impossible after this trauma, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear link to the accidental-injury context; the dominant themes would more plausibly be guilt, responsibility, or fear of causing harm again. It is weaker than the perpetrator-cue problem but still clinically questionable here.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another, unless there was also significant injury or disfigurement to the patient; no other selected items indicate patient bodily injury, making this appraisal clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used as distraction is not impossible, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other items emphasize guilt, threat vigilance, and cue-triggered distress related to the accident, whereas self-harm implies a severe affect-regulation strategy not supported elsewhere in the selected items. This strategy is therefore clinically poorly anchored in the presented formulation/profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, a burnt smell implies a fire/burning context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no matching memory content or appraisal theme tied to smoke/fire, this trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People are not what they seem' suggests interpersonal mistrust/paranoia, which is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile centered on guilt and failure to protect after accidentally injuring another person. It does not connect plausibly to the listed triggers or strategies and is not supported by any interpersonal threat content.

vignette:
At fifty-six, Leo had spent over three decades as a professional dancer, first with a contemporary company and later as a freelance choreographer and instructor. The accident happened during a rehearsal for a small, experimental piece. He had been demonstrating a lift, a partner work sequence he had performed hundreds of times, when his partner, a younger dancer named Elena, lost her balance. He tried to catch her, but his hand missed her wrist and caught her shoulder at an odd angle, and she fell hard, her head striking the edge of the wooden stage. He heard the sound of the impact. There was a lot of blood. The paramedics came, and at the hospital they said she had a fractured skull and a subdural hematoma. She survived, but she had to stop dancing. Her career was over.

In the weeks that followed, Leo could not stop replaying the moment - the sound, the angle of her body, the way his hand had failed. He became convinced that he should have done more, that he had failed in his most important role: to protect his partner, to keep her safe. He told himself that a real dancer, a real man, would have caught her. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, even though he knew, logically, that it had been a split-second mistake. These thoughts came most powerfully when he heard certain songs - the track they had been rehearsing to, or any music with a similar rhythm. The melody would start in a coffee shop or a grocery store, and he would feel the guilt rise up in his chest, hot and immediate, as if the accident were happening again. The guilt, in turn, made him more alert to those sounds; he began scanning for them, bracing himself before entering any room with a speaker.

He tried hard not to think about the trauma. He suppressed the images, pushed the thoughts away, but the effort left him exhausted and on edge. He could not relax, even at home in his own living room, where he knew he was safe. He had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, as if something bad might happen if he let his guard down. His concentration suffered; he would lose the thread of a conversation or find himself staring at a page without reading it. He began to avoid going anywhere near the theater where the accident had happened, taking a longer route to the studio where he still taught, a route that added twenty minutes to his commute. He dwelled on how he used to be before the event - the dancer who trusted his body, who moved through crowded rehearsal spaces with ease. Now, crowded spaces felt dangerous, overwhelming; he could not predict where people would be, and he found himself flinching when someone moved too quickly near him. This hypervigilance only made the crowded studio feel more threatening, and he would arrive already tense, scanning the room for potential hazards.

The cycle tightened over months. His guilt told him he was a failure, and so he watched for signs that he might fail again - a student losing balance, a dancer stumbling, a car in the parking lot moving too fast. He had come to believe that if he was not constantly vigilant, he would cause another injury, and that belief drove his avoidance and his suppression, which left him more agitated and more sensitive to any trigger. He stopped accepting new choreography commissions. He turned down a teaching residency. His wife told him he seemed distant, that he was not sleeping, that he was always on edge. He knew she was right, but he did not know how to stop. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in class: a student wobbled during a turn, and Leo froze. He could not speak. He stood there, heart pounding, for what felt like a full minute, while the class watched him. Afterward, he went home and told his wife he needed to see someone. He was most afraid that he would never trust his own body again, and that he had already lost the person he used to be.
